The zero conditional is used to express:
The zero conditional (if + present, present) states facts and general truths.

The first conditional is used for:
The first conditional (if + present, will + base) describes a real or likely future possibility.
If it rains, we ___ the match.
The first conditional uses 'will + base verb' in the main clause.
If she ___ hard, she will pass the examination.
In the first conditional, the if-clause uses the simple present, not 'will'.
The second conditional is used for:
The second conditional (if + past, would + base) describes imaginary or unlikely present situations.
If I ___ rich, I would buy a house near the sea.
The second conditional uses 'were' for all subjects in formal English.
If I knew her number, I ___ her immediately.
The second conditional uses 'would + base verb' in the main clause.
The third conditional is used for:
The third conditional (if + past perfect, would have + past participle) describes unreal past situations.
If he ___ harder, he would have passed the examination.
The third conditional uses the past perfect in the if-clause.
If I had known about the meeting, I ___ you.
The third conditional uses 'would have + past participle' in the main clause.
If I had taken the job, I ___ in London now.
This is a mixed conditional: a past condition with a present result, so 'would + base' is used.
If she were more organised, she ___ the report yesterday.
This is a mixed conditional: a present condition with a past result, so 'would have + past participle' is used.
